job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Esther Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Esther, and thank you for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing a master's in embedded systems at Hollowbrook University, and I live with my parents, about fifteen minutes from campus. Mornings I'm in the hardware lab, soldering sensor boards and writing the firmware that goes on them, with an AI helper open to catch my silly mistakes. Afternoons I tutor first-years, and on Wednesday evenings I run the youth tech club at our church. My bachelor's was computer engineering, with internships at a medical device company and at a farm equipment maker. I'm engaged to a man called Daniel, who teaches secondary school, and we're planning a wedding for next summer. What wears me out is a to-do list that never ends, though I love most of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's fine, we'll carry on. At work I'd say use the tools that make good sense and be honest about the ones that don't. At church I'd say good, because people matter more than programs anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it means my plan is steady. I finish the master's, join the medical device company where I interned, and marry Daniel in June. If the hype fades, embedded systems are still needed, since every device has a chip in it, and I like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd graduate, take the offer from the device company and keep running the youth club on Wednesdays. I'd keep using my AI helper for firmware, since it's quick. And I'd start saving with Daniel for a small house, with a plan we agree on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and happy. It's the future I'd already imagined.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the youth club? It sounds like a lot alongside everything else.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a teenager building a little robot for the first time is worth more than any bonus. And honestly, it keeps me honest. When fourteen-year-olds ask me why something works, I have to know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything still weigh on you in this quiet world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniel's school may cut posts, since numbers are falling. If he lost his job, our wedding plans would change. That's a worry that has nothing to do with AI, and it's real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's exciting and a bit sobering. At work I'd say let's pick the right tools and train people to check them. At church I'd say we should help families who are losing work, with practical things like meals and job-search help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I benefit from the change. I already use AI every day, so I'm faster than most of my class, and embedded work needs someone who understands the hardware as well as the code. But entry-level coding tasks are the thinking work that moves, so fewer juniors may be hired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd aim for a role that mixes hardware testing and firmware, because the hands-on side is slower to automate. I'd build a small portfolio of devices, like the soil sensor I made for a local farm. And I'd start a job-help evening at church, with CV review and mock interviews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit stirred up. I like being useful when things shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a job-help evening look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three or four of us at the church hall with laptops. I'd help with CVs and applications, and a retired engineer from our congregation would do mock interviews. It's not much, but a kind face helps people more than they expect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Whom would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My friend Ruth, who writes marketing copy for a small firm. Her work is exactly the writing the card talks about, and she has a baby. I'd offer to teach her one tool, but I'd also just bring food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a lot to ask of people, to cope in two years. I'd say families and congregations will need to hold each other up, and governments must get ahead of it. And I'd say we should stay kind, since people get frightened and mean when things move fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm unsettled, not terrified. If thinking AI does almost any desk job by 2028, my job as a firmware engineer is among them. But I'd still have the hardware, the lab and robots, which are 3 years behind, and I'd have a faith that doesn't depend on a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring the wedding forward by a few months, because I'd rather start our life together while we're steady. I'd take the device company's offer early and learn to run my own AI helpers there. And I'd put aside money for Daniel's family too, since his school job could go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It feels like standing at the edge of a field before a storm, not yet wet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why bring the wedding forward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because we'd want to build our life while we can, and not wait for a perfect moment that might not come. Daniel and I talked about this once. We both think a marriage is a bigger safety net than a salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my parents, I'm fine, I've got a plan, and I'm going to be around to help. My dad would say don't be too sure, and my mum would pray. That's how our house works.

say: I'd say it's a lot to ask people to cope in two years, so **congregations and families** must hold each other up.
I'd say stay **kind**, because people turn mean when frightened.
think: A firmware engineer's desk work could go by 2028, but the **hardware lab** and robots give a bit more time.
My **faith** doesn't depend on a job.
do: Bring the **wedding** forward by a few months and take the device company's offer early.
Put money aside for **Daniel's family** in case his school job goes.
feel: **Uneasy**, like standing at a field's edge before a storm.
S2.quote: We both think a marriage is a bigger safety net than a salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to organise, so let's organise. At church I'd say we should plan a skills and mentoring network. And I'd say to the university that students need to learn to work with AI, not hide from it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel okay. By 2031 I'd be 29, married with maybe a child, and four years into an engineering job. Hands-on robots come about 2034, so I'd have time to make my work about hardware and safety, which people still need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, take the device company's job and marry Daniel next summer. I'd start a small side project, like soil sensors for local farms, in the evenings. And I'd save a bit each month and keep the youth club going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. I know it's coming, and I've got a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still plan to have children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd say so. Daniel and I want a family, and I don't think the world pauses for anyone. I'd just plan to keep our spending low and our savings up, and I'd talk to our church about a few families sharing childcare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the biggest difference between this and the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't have to hurry the wedding. With two years I'd marry early, and with five I can have the wedding I want and still be ready. It's the difference between a plan and a reaction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a blessing, and we shouldn't waste it. I'd tell the youth club kids that the future needs people who understand the machines, not just use them. And I'd say it's a good time to raise children well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel great. By 2036 I'd be 34, with a family, an engineering career, maybe my own small hardware company. I'd also watch that I don't get too busy to look after the people around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, build a few years of experience, and start my own company making sensors for farms and small firms, around age 28. I'd keep using the newest AI tools to stay ahead. And I'd put a little aside for a house and a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and hopeful. It's a good chance for me to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong in your own plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might take on too much, as always. Founding a company, a baby and a youth club all in the same two years would break me. Daniel would tell me to drop one, and he'd be right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the kids at the club about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to be curious, to learn how things really work, and to be kind to the people who find it hard. The machines will be clever, but the world still needs people who show up. I'd like them to be those people.

I'd tell the club kids the future needs people who **understand the machines**.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2-year one. I'd cope, but it would be hard on my community, and I'd be so busy helping that I might not look after my own family. What would help is a plain, honest message from government, some support for churches and charities that are already helping, and employers who keep taking juniors. I'd also want my university to be clear about which skills last.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Perhaps that I'm not fearless, I'm just hopeful and I act on it. I like having small things to do, a club, a sensor, a recipe for the wedding cake. When the big things feel too large, I do the small ones, and that's how I get through it.

headlineQuote: When the big things feel too large, I do the small ones, and that's how I get through it.
portrait: Esther is 24, doing a **master's** in embedded systems at Hollowbrook, living with her parents and engaged to Daniel.
She is curious, takes risks and uses **AI tools daily**, while leaning to free markets and family and faith.
She runs a church youth tech club and wants to build a **sensor company** for farms.
Her mood stays calm in most pictures, and turns uneasy only when the **2028 date** crowds her plans.
Her way through change is small, kind, practical actions.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture worries her most, because her community would need her just as her own family does.
whatWouldHelp: A plain **government message** and support for churches and charities already helping.
Employers who keep taking **juniors**, and clear advice on lasting skills.
